name: Daria Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. This is confidential. How does your workday usually begin?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria Abbott, forty-three, and I start with the client ledger before I open the email. At Beckett & Hall I prepare accounts and tax returns for repair shops and small landlords, then call when a receipt does not fit. I have a bachelor's in accounting and a professional accountancy qualification, and I've handled ordinary returns for years. I don't use AI tools; the paper working file still tells me where a number came from.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears on you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a client who tells me the truth about a muddled bill. I get tired of late records and the firm's low pay for experienced work. My partner Ben is a carpenter whose contracts come in blocks, our children are eight and fourteen, and we have a mortgage. We have less than a month of expenses saved and few similar accounting firms nearby, so I guard the wage we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds manageable. The firm has a new sorting screen, but I still work from the ledger and the client folder; I have never used the AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients their return will still be checked by a qualified person. I'd say at work that a few saved minutes ought to make filing week kinder, not become another target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, our worry is the mortgage rather than a new tool. I'm forty-three and experienced with accounts and returns, but Beckett & Hall pays me below the usual rate. My partner Ben's carpentry contracts vary, our two children are at school, and we have less than one month saved with few similar firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my ledger review and the client calls I know. This month I'd cancel the magazine subscription and leave its twelve in the household bill account. In the first year of a plateau, I'd keep the same tax clients and ask the partners for a written pay review after the filing season, without counting a raise before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary bills, even if my work holds. A canceled contract for Ben can wipe out our spare money in one week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What emptied the savings last time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The roof needed a small repair last spring, and Ben did the work but we still paid for timber. The last savings went to the timber bill. I kept a paper envelope for emergencies after that, but there is almost nothing in it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you ask for a raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take my client renewals and error record to the pay meeting. If the partners refuse, I'll keep the job while asking about real vacancies elsewhere. I won't tell the children we can afford a trip on an unsigned pay promise.

say: I would keep **qualified checks** on every tax return before it reaches a client.
I would ask that saved time ease **filing pressure**.
think: Our **mortgage** worries me even when this firm keeps the same hours.
Ben’s **variable contracts** make our thin reserve fragile.
do: Keep **ledger reviews** and familiar client calls.
Cancel the **magazine subscription** and hold twelve for bills.
Request a **written pay review** after filing season.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary household bills.
S0.quote: The last savings went to the timber bill.
fieldNote: The **timber bill** explains a thin cushion despite her experience and professional qualification.
Her **paper ledger routine** remains central; she has never used AI at work.

steps.text: Keep ledger review and calls for current tax clients
Cancel magazine subscription and hold twelve monthly for bills
Request pay review; if refused keep current pay while asking about real vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking, writing and answering clients are the substance of my week. If the software handles those, the partners could keep the same client list with fewer accounting hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to say which hours might go and when. I'd tell friends that a person who trained for this work deserves a fair chance to move, not a cheerful notice on the last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own weekly pay could lose a full day after the next filing season. That would be a big cut with our mortgage and Ben's uncertain contracts, and I have little cash to bridge it. I know these clients, but I have not learned the AI tools the partners prefer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask two colleagues to sign a request for the staffing plan at the next team meeting. I'd bring my signed returns and client renewals to show what still needs a person. If the partners cut a day, I'd apply for the funded parish-school bursar post only if its published wage covers our mortgage, its start is fixed and the school-run hours work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a large cut in our main wage. I lie awake thinking which bill would be late first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner’s work really guarantee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben's next carpentry contract is signed for six weeks, not a year. I would not tell him to take more work until a client has offered it. We'd cut the children's paid holiday club before letting the mortgage go late, though that would make school breaks hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the school post solve the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school post has to be a real vacancy with pay on the advert. If the start date or hours are vague, I keep Beckett & Hall's pay and ask family about holiday childcare while looking. I do not move for a title alone.

say: I would demand a **dated staffing plan** before the partners remove a paid day.
I would ask for a **fair paid move** before cuts.
think: I expect a **full day** of pay could go after the next filing season.
Ben’s **short contracts** cannot replace that wage.
do: Ask **two colleagues** to sign a staffing-plan request at the team meeting.
Cut **paid holiday club** before mortgage arrears; ask family about holiday childcare while retaining current pay if job terms fail.
Apply for **funded school work** after a day cut only with written mortgage pay, start and hours; otherwise keep current pay.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a large wage cut.
S1.quote: I do not move for a title alone.
fieldNote: She expects a **full-day reduction**, making alarm consistent with her thin cushion and variable second income.
The **bursar fallback** requires an advertised funded vacancy, mortgage-covering pay, fixed start and school-run hours.

steps.text: Bring signed returns and renewals with two colleagues to seek written staffing plan
Cut paid holiday club before allowing mortgage arrears
Seek funded bursar after day cut with written mortgage wage/start/school hours; otherwise retain pay
Ask family about holiday childcare while searching if bursar terms remain vague

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 is too fast for a family to rearrange its mortgage and school life. A cheaper system that can do almost all thinking work would take the returns I have built my week around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for notice and an honest wage bridge, though I don't like being dependent on support. I'd tell the partners not to leave experienced staff guessing about when their last paid day comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my accounting job to end in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028. My work is mainly thinking at a desk, so robots around 2031 do not add years to this job. Ben's hands-on carpentry could last longer, but robots later might reach it, and his signed six-week contract won't pay this mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the paid after-school club after this term and hold its eighty each month for bills. I'd ask my sister to cover one school pickup each week only if she agrees to the actual day. In the first year after 2028, if Beckett & Hall dismisses me, I'd claim temporary wage support and call the lender before missing a mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I know how to make a list, but I cannot list our way into a second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your sister manage school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister has two children of her own, so I would ask rather than assume. If she cannot cover a pickup, I would keep the after-school club until another arrangement is confirmed. I won't leave the children at a school gate to save a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lender gets a call with our mortgage statement and the last payslip, not a story about possible carpentry work. I'd ask for temporary terms and a written answer. I would keep paying the regular amount while I still had wages.

say: I would seek **notice and temporary wages** while our household finds a replacement job.
I would demand a **last-day date** from the firm.
think: My **desk job** may end soon after 2028, before our family can save more.
Ben’s **carpentry income** may last longer but remains uncertain.
do: Stop **after-school club** only after replacement pickup is confirmed, keeping eighty monthly for bills.
Ask the **lender** for written temporary terms before missing payment.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing our main wage.
S2.quote: I won't leave the children at a school gate to save a bill.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches her accounting desk in 2028, while carpentry faces later robot risk.
The **after-school club cut** depends on confirmed childcare, and support is a reluctant bridge.

steps.text: Cancel after-school club after term only with confirmed replacement pickup; retain eighty monthly for bills
Claim temporary wage support after 2028 job loss
Ask lender for written temporary mortgage terms before missed payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us time to see which employers still pay people to work with customers. I would still expect my tax returns to change sharply when full AGI arrives in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm to train people for real posts and give them notice, not make them buy a course on faith. I'd ask for a wage during any transition, because family bills arrive every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might work at my brother's builders' merchant on the counter, where I know the products and can explain an invoice. Robots arrive around 2034, so I wouldn't call hands-on counter work permanent safety. The tax desk is exposed in 2031, and I need the merchant to have an actual funded place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask my brother's manager about a paid counter trial on two Saturdays, only if Beckett & Hall agrees to my schedule and the merchant pays for the hours. I'd keep my accounting pay while trying it. In the first year after AGI in 2031, if my tax job ends, I'd take a funded merchant post only if its written wage covers our mortgage and its start and school hours are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can ask about a real shift without betting the house. The store would have to pay me, not just call it family help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the manager rather than your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the manager, not my brother, for the wage and dates. If the two Saturdays are unpaid, I won't go and I'll keep my current clients. A family connection is not a payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to learn at the counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can help a customer choose a fitting from the shelf, but I would need to learn the till and stock numbers. If the trial goes ahead, I'd ask a paid colleague to show me the morning routine. I won't claim I know the job from one visit.

say: I would seek **real paid posts** before training.
I would ask for a **transition wage** while families adjust.
think: A **merchant counter** might offer a short bridge after my tax desk closes.
Robots in **2034** could reach hands-on work too.
do: Test **two paid Saturdays** only with both employers’ agreement.
Keep **accounting pay** if the counter trial is unpaid.
Take a **funded merchant post** after 2031 loss only with mortgage wage and hours.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but able to test a real shift.
S3.quote: A family connection is not a payslip.
fieldNote: A **paid counter trial** uses an existing family connection without making a family favour the wage plan.
She explicitly sees the **2034 robot date** as limiting the counter role after AGI reaches accounting.

steps.text: Test two paid merchant Saturdays only if both employers approve
Keep accounting clients and wage if merchant trial is unpaid
Take funded merchant job after 2031 tax loss only with written mortgage wage, start, school hours
Learn merchant till and stock numbers with paid colleague if paid trial goes ahead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would put the children much closer to adulthood, but I don't want to spend those years waiting for a notice. I would be fifty-three in 2036 and still need wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask firms to use some of the savings to keep apprenticeships open and pay for orderly job moves. I'd tell friends that family help is useful, but no family should be expected to replace a full wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the return desk will be smaller or gone when thinking AI arrives in 2036. I could work in a merchant's customer area before that, but robots around 2039 may reach the hands-on parts too. A funded employer and pay that covers the mortgage matter more than a hopeful story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my client accounts now and add twenty monthly to the emergency envelope only if Ben's signed contract pays on time. Next spring I'd ask the builders' merchant for a published paid opening and a school-compatible rota, without leaving Beckett & Hall. In the first year after 2036, if the tax role ends, I'd take the merchant job only if its written wage covers our mortgage and the start is confirmed; otherwise I'd seek temporary support and keep looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the thin envelope, even with a decade. Ten years helps me ask better questions, but it does not refill our emergency envelope today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with bills by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child could be working by then, but I would not plan to use her wage. She should build her own life. I want the children to remember us making careful choices, not passing our bills to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the merchant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the merchant for the advertised wage, the shift times and who is responsible for training. If it has no funded opening, I keep the accounting wage and ask again later. I won't turn a conversation in the shop into a career change.

say: I would seek **paid orderly moves** and apprenticeships.
I would value **family help** without treating it as wages.
think: My **return desk** still faces AGI in 2036.
The **merchant role** needs real pay before robot risk in 2039.
do: Save **twenty monthly** only after Ben’s signed contract pays.
Check **funded merchant openings** while keeping accounting pay.
Take a **mortgage-covering merchant post** after 2036 loss; otherwise seek support.
feel: I feel **anxious** about our thin cash envelope.
S4.quote: Ten years helps me ask better questions, but it does not refill our emergency envelope today.
fieldNote: The **conditional twenty** is new cash only after a signed carpentry contract pays.
She keeps **current accounting pay** while checking a merchant opening and acknowledges 2039 robot exposure.

steps.text: Add twenty monthly only after signed carpentry contract pays
Check funded merchant openings while keeping current accounting wage
Take funded merchant post after 2036 tax loss if written mortgage wage, start, hours fit
Seek temporary support after 2036 tax loss if no funded merchant post

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My tax desk could go before we have enough cash for one month, and Ben's work is booked only weeks ahead. Clear notice, a temporary wage bridge, lender flexibility and a funded job with written pay would help. I would rather take a paid shift than ask family to carry our mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a family can promise a child. I can tell ours we will try to keep the house, but I can't promise a new job before somebody offers the hours and wage. That is why I want the details on paper.

headlineQuote: I would rather take a paid shift than ask family to carry our mortgage.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Daria prepares repair-shop accounts and tax returns at Beckett & Hall.
Her **accounting degree** and professional qualification support midlevel skill, despite below-usual pay.
She **never uses AI**, preferring a paper working file and direct client calls.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and less than one month saved make pay cuts frightening.
Few **nearby firms** lead her to require funded shifts, written wages and confirmed school hours.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her desk role before the family saves one month of expenses.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **notice**, a temporary wage bridge, lender flexibility and funded work with written pay.
